newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac says Europeanising NATO still difficult.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says Europeanising NATO still difficult.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday that essential problems remained to be solved to give European allies their rightful role in the NATO alliance.
Addressing the Western European Union (WEU) parliamentary assembly, Chirac said the U.S.-led Atlantic Alliance had made progress towards giving Europe a bigger role in its own defence.

But he said: "Let us not hide it, there remain essential and very difficult points...to be resolved, notably the Europeanisation of the regional commands. Solving these problems is obviously indispensible to complete the reform successfully."

He was referring to a dispute over French demands, rejected by Washington, that the United States hand over NATO's Southern Command in Naples, which controls allied forces in the Mediterranean and Bosnia, to a European officer.
In a letter to President Bill Clinton in October, obtained by Reuters, Chirac said the matter was of "capital importance".
In his WEU speech, Chirac did not repeat recent threats by Paris to freeze its reintegration into NATO's military structure if it does not obtain satisfaction on the AFSOUTH issue.
But he did say: "Completion of the reform of the Alliance would make it possible to reconcile our European and Atlantic ambitions, which for too long have been artificially opposed."
Declaring that "Europe must put an end to its impotence", Chirac said he would use France's presidency of the WEU next year to reinforce the 10-nation European defence grouping.
He said Paris would propose improvements in coordination with the European Union, which could be enshrined in amendments to the WEU's founding treaty when it comes up for renewal in 1998.

The 1991 Maastricht treaty designated the WEU as the future defence arm of the European Union, but Britain has since opposed bringing the defence grouping under the authority of the EU's summit of heads of state and government.
And diplomats said most WEU states appear to prefer simply rolling over the Brussels Treaty rather than adding amendments that would require parliamentary ratification.
It was the first time a French president had addressed the WEU parliamentary assembly, a gesture which underlined Chirac's support for a stronger European defence identity.

"The WEU must seize the opportunity it has been given to assert itself both as the expression of a real European identity within the (NATO) Alliance and as the defence component of the European Union," he said.

Chirac spelled out four priorities for reinforcing the WEU's capabilities: boosting its military planning cell, developing a European military spy satellite programme, coordinating existing multinational European forces better through the WEU and building a competitve European defence industry.
